idiom_name: static of()/valueOf() factory method with a private constructor
implementation_notes: Java's everyday factory is a static method such as of/valueOf/getInstance/newX that chooses the implementation and may return a cached instance (Integer.valueOf) or an implementation hidden behind an interface (List.of), while constructors stay private or package-private. Effective Java's first item recommends exactly this because a static factory can have a descriptive name, return a subtype and reuse instances - none of which a constructor can do. The classic abstract Creator with an overridable create() remains for framework hooks where a subclass must supply composed products.
pitfalls: Static factory methods are not inherited and cannot be overridden, so a factory that must vary per subclass needs the instance (virtual) form instead.

Classes without a public constructor cannot be subclassed or instantiated by frameworks that require one (some serializers, reflection-based containers, JPA) - keep a protected constructor where that applies.
A factory returning a cached instance makes identity assumptions unsafe (== versus equals) and adds shared mutable state if the cached object is not immutable.
sources: Bloch, Effective Java (3rd ed.), Item 1: Consider static factory methods instead of constructors.

variants.name: Map of Supplier<T> creators
variants.implementation_notes: The functional-style Java realization: the creator set is a Map<String, Supplier<Product>> (or a Map<String, Function<Config, Product>> when creation takes arguments), so creation is a value that can be assembled, filtered and injected. It replaces the Creator hierarchy for the common case where the decision is a lookup, and it composes well with dependency injection: the map is built once at the composition root and the factory is a method that consults it.
pitfalls: Map.of and Map.copyOf reject null keys/values and are immutable - a registry that plugins extend must be built once at startup or guarded explicitly.
Suppliers that capture mutable configuration freeze the value at registration time; decide whether the product should see later configuration changes.
Lambdas give poor stack traces for creation failures; wrap the invocation if you need to know which key failed.
sources: Bloch, Effective Java (3rd ed.), Item 1: Consider static factory methods instead of constructors.

variants.name: ServiceLoader providers declared per module or META-INF/services
variants.implementation_notes: For pluggable implementations the JDK itself provides the factory mechanism: the application calls ServiceLoader.load(Service.class), and each provider module declares its implementation in module-info (provides ... with ...) or in META-INF/services, optionally exposing a public static no-arg provider() method instead of a public no-arg constructor. The host code refers only to the service interface and chooses among the providers it finds, which is the runtime-selection case of the pattern realized by the platform rather than by a hand-written creator.
pitfalls: Providers are instantiated through a public no-arg constructor or a static provider() method only; a provider that needs configuration must receive it in create(), like the CodecFactory example in the javadoc.
A module that calls ServiceLoader.load must declare uses ..., and a missing provider is silent at compile time and only visible as an empty result at run time.
ServiceLoader instances cache providers; reload() is needed to see newly deployed providers, and iteration order is not a contract - sort or filter explicitly.
